The second great outbreak of cholera, which spread out of Bengal in 1826 and reached Europe by 1830. It was the first time the disease struck Europe on a large scale, and it shaped how cities thought about dirt, water and public health for the rest of the century.

The disease moved along trade and pilgrim routes, through Afghanistan and Persia into the Russian Empire. It hit Moscow in 1830, then followed armies into Poland during the uprising of 1830 and 1831 and spread to Prussia, Austria and Hungary. Britain had its first cases at Sunderland in late 1831. Paris lost thousands in the spring of 1832, among them the prime minister Casimir Perier. Ships carried it across the Atlantic to Quebec and New York the same year.

Nobody yet knew how it spread. Many blamed bad air, the poor or foreigners, and there were cholera riots in Russia and Britain. The fear pushed governments to set up boards of health, and it set the stage for later work on clean water. It followed the earlier first pandemic, which had stopped short of Europe, and Russia was its gateway as part of the Russian Empire.
